clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in SCN1B, which encodes the beta1 auxiliary subunit of the voltage-gated sodium channel that modulates channel gating, trafficking, and cell adhesion
Heterozygous variants classically cause genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+), an autosomal dominant familial spectrum with variable severity
Biallelic (homozygous or compound heterozygous) loss-of-function variants can cause a severe early infantile Dravet-like developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
The GEFS+ spectrum includes simple febrile seizures, febrile seizures persisting beyond the usual age, and afebrile generalised or focal seizures within the same family
Fever sensitivity and prolonged seizures are recurrent features, overlapping clinically with SCN1A-related disorders

Because the beta subunit modulates neuronal sodium channels, disturbed channel function alters excitability, and antiseizure choice should account for the Dravet-like overlap where sodium-channel blockers may be poorly tolerated in the severe phenotype
The severe biallelic phenotype carries developmental impairment and, as with related sodium-channel epilepsies, attention to sudden unexpected death in epilepsy risk
reference.pathophysiology: SCN1B encodes the beta1 subunit of the voltage-gated sodium channel, an auxiliary transmembrane protein that regulates the gating kinetics, surface trafficking, and localisation of the pore-forming alpha subunits and also functions as a cell-adhesion molecule influencing neuronal development. Heterozygous variants partially disturb sodium channel behaviour and produce the variable GEFS+ spectrum, while complete loss of beta1 function from biallelic variants more profoundly deranges channel regulation, resulting in the severe Dravet-like encephalopathy. The consequent instability of neuronal firing, particularly under the stress of fever, lowers the seizure threshold and, in the severe form, impairs the developing brain.
additionalDifferentials: SCN1A and GABRG2 febrile seizure spectrum disorders
Other genetic causes of febrile-seizure-associated epilepsy
additionalInvestigations: Epilepsy gene panel or whole-exome sequencing, noting zygosity to distinguish GEFS+ from the biallelic Dravet-like phenotype
Electroencephalography to characterise generalised and focal features
Brain magnetic resonance imaging to exclude structural causes in severe presentations
Detailed family history and segregation analysis for the dominant GEFS+ spectrum
Developmental assessment in the severe phenotype
redFlags: Prolonged febrile-triggered seizures or febrile status epilepticus
Developmental regression in the biallelic Dravet-like phenotype
Features suggesting sudden unexpected death in epilepsy risk
reference.prognosis: Heterozygous GEFS+ often has a favourable outcome with age-limited febrile seizures and normal cognition, whereas the biallelic Dravet-like encephalopathy carries drug-resistant seizures and developmental impairment.
pitfalls: Not checking zygosity, which distinguishes the mild dominant spectrum from severe recessive disease
Applying sodium-channel-blocker therapy indiscriminately in the Dravet-like phenotype
Anchoring on SCN1A and missing SCN1B in a GEFS+ family
Underestimating fever sensitivity and prolonged-seizure risk
references: GeneReviews and OMIM resources on SCN1B-related epilepsy and GEFS+
ILAE resources on genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus
management: Control seizures in the severe phenotype with broad-spectrum antiseizure medication such as sodium valproate, levetiracetam, or clobazam
Use sodium-channel-blocking agents cautiously in the biallelic Dravet-like phenotype, where they may be poorly tolerated
Treat fever promptly with antipyretics, since fever lowers the seizure threshold and provokes prolonged seizures
Provide a rescue benzodiazepine protocol for prolonged seizures and counsel families on managing status epilepticus
Undertake developmental surveillance and early intervention in the severe encephalopathy
Offer genetic counselling with family segregation analysis, distinguishing dominant GEFS+ from biallelic disease
Refer to paediatric neurology and epileptology for phenotype-guided drug selection
